pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — 7–9; know the Amazon is Earth's greatest rainforest — spanning nine South American countries, holding the world's largest river by volume, and home to an estimated 10% of all known species (40,000 plants, 1,300 birds, 3,000 fish).
• Standards — UK: DfE KS2 Geography (locate world regions, countries, rivers; use maps/atlases) and Science 'Living things and their habitats' (a specific biome case study).
• Standards — US: NGSS/social-studies geography (locate major regions and rivers) and 3-LS4-3/biodiversity-of-place.
• Operational details — make it a MAP + RECORD-BREAKER topic: locate the Amazon on South America, name two countries it spans (Brazil, Peru…), and attach the superlatives to concrete comparisons that mean something to a child ('largest river by volume' = more water than the next several biggest rivers combined; '10% of all species' = 1 in every 10 kinds of living thing on Earth lives here). Keep numbers as awe-anchors, not rote figures; ground each stat visually.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (7): find the Amazon on a map and name two countries. Tier B (8): state that it has the world's largest river by volume and ~10% of Earth's species. Tier C (9): cite two specific biodiversity numbers (40,000 plants / 1,300 birds) and explain what '10% of all species' really means.
bestPractices: Anchor every superlative to a concrete comparison a child can picture (river vs Nile+Mississippi bars; 10% = 1 in 10 Earths).
Start from the map — locate it, name countries — before the statistics, so the numbers have a place to live.
Use the awe of records to drive engagement, but keep two memorable numbers rather than a long list.
Connect to prior 'Where Rainforests Are' knowledge (the Amazon is THE South American rainforest).
Foreshadow later topics lightly: this incredible richness is exactly what deforestation threatens.
keyRepresentations: A map of South America with the Amazon basin shaded and countries labelled.
The great river drawn thick, with comparison bars against other major rivers.
Biodiversity record cards (40,000 plants, 1,300 birds, 3,000 fish).
A '10 Earths' proportion visual shading one to show 10% of all species.
commonMisconceptions: 'The Amazon is one country / in Brazil only' — it spans nine countries.
'The Amazon is the LONGEST river' — the claim taught here is largest by WATER VOLUME/discharge (Nile length is debated separately).
'10% of species means 10 species' — it means one tenth of ALL kinds of living things on Earth.
'A rainforest and its river are the same thing' — the forest is the habitat; the river runs through it.
'These numbers are exact and fixed' — they are estimates; many species remain undiscovered.

learn.summary: For ages 7–9, learners locate the Amazon on a map of South America, name at least two of the nine countries it spans, and connect its record-breaking statistics (world's largest river by water volume; roughly 10% of all known species; ~40,000 plants, ~1,300 birds, ~3,000 fish) to concrete comparisons they can picture. The teaching sequence starts from the map (giving the numbers 'a place to live') before attaching awe-anchoring superlatives. Core misconceptions to confront: the Amazon as a single country/only-Brazil, 'largest river' meaning longest rather than greatest water volume, and '10% of species' meaning 10 species rather than one tenth of all kinds of life. These figures are estimates, not fixed exact counts.

activities.title: Find it on the map, then name the countries
feedback: If a learner calls the Amazon a country or says it's only in Brazil, point back to the map: it's a rainforest that spans nine South American countries — trace its edges across more than one.
If a learner conflates the forest and the river, clarify: the forest is the habitat; the river runs through it.
Confirm correct country names against the map and invite them to find a second or third country they didn't expect.
activities.rationale: Grounding the facts in map location first gives the later statistics a concrete place to attach to, and directly targets the common 'Amazon is a country' misconception. KS2 geography expects locating world regions, countries and major rivers using maps and atlases.
sourceClaims: The Amazon spans nine countries in South America, contains the world's largest river by discharge/volume, and is estimated to hold around 10% of all known species on Earth
KS2 geography requires locating world regions, countries and major rivers using maps and atlases
learnerActions: Locate the shaded Amazon basin on a map of South America.
Name at least two countries the Amazon spreads across (e.g. Brazil, Peru, Colombia).
State in your own words that the Amazon is a rainforest spanning nine South American countries — not a single country and not only Brazil.
activities.intendedInsight: The Amazon is Earth's greatest rainforest that crosses nine countries; it is a habitat, not a nation, and the river runs through the forest rather than being the same thing as it.

activities.title: Largest by water, not by length
feedback: If a learner justifies 'largest' only by length, redirect: here 'largest' means the most water carried (volume/discharge), not how long the river is.
Use the comparison bars to let them see the Amazon's bar dwarf the others and put the difference in their own words.
activities.rationale: Explicitly separating volume from length heads off the 'largest = longest' confusion, and a volume comparison bar makes an abstract superlative into something a child can picture. Which river is longest is a separate and debated question and is not the claim being taught here.
sourceClaims: The Amazon spans nine countries in South America, contains the world's largest river by discharge/volume, and is estimated to hold around 10% of all known species on Earth
learnerActions: Consider the question 'Which river carries the most water on Earth?' and predict before the answer is shown.
Compare a thick bar representing the Amazon's water volume against bars for other major rivers (e.g. Nile, Mississippi) and describe what 'largest' means here.
State clearly that the Amazon is the largest river by water volume (discharge), and explain why this is different from being the longest.
activities.intendedInsight: 'Largest river' in this topic means greatest water volume/discharge — the Amazon moves more water than the next several giant rivers combined — which is a distinct claim from how long a river is.

activities.title: What '10% of all species' really means
feedback: If a learner reads '10% of species' as '10 species', use the ten-Earths visual, where all ten pictures together stand for every known kind of life: shading one of the ten shows one tenth of ALL kinds of life. That is a huge number of distinct types, far more than 10. The plants alone are about 40,000 kinds.
If a learner says only 'many animals', push for variety: tens of thousands of different plant and animal types, not just high numbers of a few.
Treat the figures as estimates — tell learners many species are still undiscovered, so these numbers are approximate, not fixed exact counts.
activities.rationale: A proportion visual makes a percentage meaningful to a 7–9 year old and directly counters both the '10 species' and 'just lots of animals' misconceptions. Framing numbers as estimates preserves scientific honesty about biodiversity counts.
sourceClaims: The Amazon spans nine countries in South America, contains the world's largest river by discharge/volume, and is estimated to hold around 10% of all known species on Earth
learnerActions: Look at a row of ten Earth pictures that together stand for all the known kinds of life on Earth, with each picture standing for one tenth. Shade one picture to show the roughly 10% of all those species that live in the Amazon.
Explain in your own words that this means roughly 1 in every 10 kinds of living thing on Earth lives here — not 10 species.
Read the record cards (about 40,000 plant species, 1,300 bird species, 3,000 types of fish) and name at least two specific biodiversity numbers.
Say why biodiversity means huge VARIETY of different kinds, not just 'lots of animals'.
activities.intendedInsight: Biodiversity is about the variety of distinct kinds of life; the Amazon holds about one tenth of all known species on Earth, an extraordinary concentration of different living things.

activities.title: Explain why the Amazon is special (diagnostic discussion)
feedback: If the learner keeps the Amazon as a country or only Brazil, reteach location on the map before the statistics.
If they say 'many animals' without variety, emphasise distinct kinds (~10% of all species).
If they give facts but no reason, prompt: what about the climate might let so many different kinds of life thrive here compared with, say, a British wood?
activities.rationale: A two-tier prompt (what is it? why is it special?) separates the child with scale/geography errors from the one who grasps a vast multi-country forest with record biodiversity; the reason-tier surfaces the biodiversity explanation. This is a proposed discussion scaffold, not a validated or uniquely effective method, and the WWF claim is cited only because the required corrected description depends on it.
sourceClaims: The Amazon spans nine countries in South America, contains the world's largest river by discharge/volume, and is estimated to hold around 10% of all known species on Earth
learnerActions: Respond to the prompt: 'Someone says the Amazon is a country in Brazil. Is that right? Tell me what the Amazon actually is, and then why it's such a special place for wildlife.'
Give a corrected description: Earth's greatest rainforest across nine South American countries, with the largest river by water volume.
Explain WHY so much life lives there — linking the richness to the hot, wet climate rather than only restating numbers.
activities.intendedInsight: A learner who understands this topic can correct the country/length/scale errors and give a reason for the Amazon's biodiversity, not just recite facts.

constraints: Start from the map (locate, name countries) before introducing statistics so the numbers have a concrete place to attach to.
Keep to a small number of memorable awe-anchor numbers rather than a long list of figures.
Present the biodiversity figures (40,000 plants, 1,300 birds, 3,000 fish, ~10% of species) as estimates; many species remain undiscovered and counts are approximate.
'Largest river' must be taught as greatest water volume/discharge, kept distinct from which river is longest, which is a separate and debated question.

Connect to prior learning about where rainforests are (the Amazon is South America's largest rainforest, though not its only one), and foreshadow lightly that this richness is what deforestation threatens.

A matching/multiple-choice end-check can assess recall and recognition of the three evidence points; recognition alone does not require the learner to explore the location or explain the scale, so pair any such check with map exploration and the proportion visuals.

Interactive tap-to-reveal maps, drag-the-country-label games, estimate-then-reveal proportion bars, comparison bars and the ten-Earths shading are useful ways to make scale concrete; they are optional illustrations, not required mechanisms — a rich printed or spoken-and-drawn version can teach the same ideas.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; both sources remain marked verified:false and were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The two cited sources support the factual content and the KS2 location requirement; they do not establish comparative efficacy of any particular medium (map vs game vs quiz vs 3D vs dialogue). No necessity or 'only this teaches' claims should be inferred.

Source figures (40,000 plants, 1,300 birds, 3,000 fish, ~10% of species, largest river by volume) and the 'nine countries' tally are attributed to a single WWF page and are estimates/conventions; treat precise counts cautiously and as approximate.

The legacy entry rated a 3D flythrough as unnecessary and open dialogue as adding nothing; these are catalog fit judgements, not established pedagogical laws. A guided dialogue is retained here as a diagnostic discussion activity because talk can support teaching and assessment, scoped as a proposal.
Activity 4's source linkage is retained only to back the required corrected factual description; the diagnostic-method claim in its rationale is not itself source-supported.

probeDeeper: Name one country the Amazon rainforest spreads across.
The Amazon has about 10% of all species on Earth — what does that tell you about how varied its life is?
What makes the Amazon River the 'largest' — is it length or something else?
Why might so many species live in the Amazon and not in, say, a British wood?
assess.correctAnswer: No — the Amazon isn't a country. It's Earth's greatest rainforest, spreading across nine countries in South America (not just Brazil), and it holds the world's largest river by water volume. It's special for wildlife because it's home to about 10% of all the species on Earth — tens of thousands of plants, over a thousand kinds of bird, thousands of fish — more variety of life than almost anywhere else.

errorPatterns.pattern: the Amazon is a country / only in Brazil — confuses the forest with a nation
errorPatterns.nextMove: it's a rainforest spanning nine South American countries; locate it on a map
errorPatterns.distractor: It's a country in South America called Amazon
errorPatterns.revealedBy: calls the Amazon a country or says it's only in Brazil

errorPatterns.pattern: 'largest river' means longest — mixes up length with water volume
errorPatterns.nextMove: the Amazon carries the most water (by volume) of any river; largest here means volume

errorPatterns.pattern: biodiversity is just 'lots of animals' — misses the huge VARIETY of different species
errorPatterns.nextMove: emphasise variety: about 10% of all species, tens of thousands of distinct plant and animal types
errorPatterns.revealedBy: says 'many animals' but not many different kinds

responseLevels.gap: Thinks the Amazon is a country or only in Brazil; 'largest river' means longest.
responseLevels.full: Describes the Amazon as Earth's greatest rainforest across nine countries with the largest river by water volume, cites its ~10% of world species as extraordinary variety, and links its richness to the hot, wet climate.
responseLevels.partial: Knows it's a huge rainforest with lots of wildlife but muddles the multi-country extent, the volume point, or the species scale.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Someone says 'the Amazon is a country in Brazil.' Is that right? Tell me what the Amazon actually is, and then tell me WHY it's such a special place for wildlife.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who thinks the Amazon is a country or only in Brazil has the scale and geography wrong; the concept child knows it's a vast multi-country forest with record biodiversity and the largest river by volume. The reason-tier surfaces the biodiversity reason.
